claim: Hybridization between species is common across the tree of life, spanning both ancient and recent timescales and a broad range of divergence levels between taxa.
source: Recent evidence has shown that hybridization between species is common. Hybridization is widespread across the tree of life, spanning both ancient and recent timescales and a broad range of divergence levels between taxa (Dobzhansky, 1982; Payseur and Rieseberg, 2016; Sankararaman et al., 2014; Schumer et al., 2016; Rieseberg et al., 1995; Teeter et al., 2008; Turissini and Matute, 2017; Káldy et al., 2020; Chae et al., 2014; Bolnick, 2009; Eberlein et al., 2019; Langdon et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2014; Delmore and Irwin, 2014; Steensels et al., 2021; Shen et al., 2018; Möller and Stukenbrock, 2017; Langdon et al., 2019; Gryganskyi et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published research documenting hybridization across diverse taxa.

claim: In humans, approximately 2-5% of the genomes of some populations are derived from ancient admixture with Neanderthals and Denisovans.
source: In humans, ~2–5% of the genomes of some populations are derived from ancient admixture with our extinct relatives, the Neanderthals and Denisovans (Sankararaman et al., 2016), including genes that contribute to adaptation and genetic diseases (Dannemann et al., 2017; Dannemann and Kelso, 2017; Enard and Petrov, 2018; Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sankararaman et al., 2016 and additional citations for functional consequences.

claim: Neanderthal and Denisovan ancestry in humans includes genes that contribute to adaptation and genetic diseases.
source: In humans, ~2–5% of the genomes of some populations are derived from ancient admixture with our extinct relatives, the Neanderthals and Denisovans (Sankararaman et al., 2016), including genes that contribute to adaptation and genetic diseases (Dannemann et al., 2017; Dannemann and Kelso, 2017; Enard and Petrov, 2018; Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting functional impacts of introgressed ancestry.

claim: In swordtail fishes, Heliconius butterflies, Italian sparrows, sunflowers, and cichlid fishes, upwards of 10% of some species' genomes are derived from ancient hybridization.
source: In other taxa, such as swordtail fishes, Heliconius butterflies, Italian sparrows, sunflowers, and cichlid fishes, upwards of 10% of some species' genomes are derived from ancient hybridization (Cui, 2013; Meier et al., 2017; Hermansen et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in multiple species groups.

claim: Adaptive introgression has been well-documented in several species.
source: Some of this genetic exchange reflects the process of adaptive introgression, which has been well-documented in several species (Marques et al., 2019; Hedrick, 2013; Racimo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published research on adaptive introgression.

claim: Introgression of adaptive and neutral variants occurs against the backdrop of broad, genome-wide selection against hybrids.
source: However, the introgression of adaptive and neutral variants occurs against the backdrop of broad, genome-wide selection against hybrids (Orr, 1995; Arnegard et al., 2014; Svedin et al., 2008; Christie and Strauss, 2018) and hybridization-derived regions in the genome (Sankararaman et al., 2014; Juric et al., 2016; Harris and Nielsen, 2016; Schumer et al., 2018; Calfee, 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting selection against hybrids and introgressed regions.

claim: The mechanisms resulting in lower fitness of hybrids are diverse, ranging from ecological selection against hybrids, to differences in the number of deleterious variants harbored by the hybridizing species (hybridization load), to negative interactions between genes derived from the two parental species' genomes (hybrid incompatibilities).
source: The mechanisms resulting in lower fitness of hybrids are diverse, ranging from ecological selection against hybrids, to differences in the number of deleterious variants harbored by the hybridizing species (known as hybridization load), to negative interactions between genes derived from the two parental species' genomes (hybrid incompatibilities).
evidence: Draws from established understanding of mechanisms of hybrid fitness reduction.

claim: On average, selection acts to remove ancestry from the minor parent in the most functionally important regions of the genome.
source: One common observation from these cases is that, on average, selection acts to remove ancestry from the minor parent (i.e., the species from which hybrids derive less of their genome) in the most functionally important regions of the genome.
evidence: Based on observations from multiple studies of local ancestry patterns.

claim: Variance in genome-wide ancestry in admixed populations is predicted to be highest just after hybridization and decreases over time as recombination breaks down long ancestry tracts.
source: Variance in genome-wide ancestry in admixed populations is predicted to be highest just after hybridization and decreases over time as recombination breaks down long ancestry tracts.
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions about ancestry dynamics after hybridization.

claim: When foreign ancestry is deleterious, selection during the initial period rapidly reduces the population's admixture proportion.
source: When foreign ancestry is deleterious, selection during this initial period rapidly reduces the population's admixture proportion (Harris and Nielsen, 2016; Veller, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on ancestry dynamics.

claim: The initial 'fast' period of purging lasts tens of generations.
source: This initial 'fast' period of purging lasts tens of generations (Veller, 2019), shifts ancestry genome-wide (Schumer et al., 2018; Matute et al., 2020), and begins to generate broad-scale differences in ancestry within and among chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and empirical studies.

claim: The initial fast period of purging shifts ancestry genome-wide and begins to generate broad-scale differences in ancestry within and among chromosomes.
source: This initial 'fast' period of purging lasts tens of generations (Veller, 2019), shifts ancestry genome-wide (Schumer et al., 2018; Matute et al., 2020), and begins to generate broad-scale differences in ancestry within and among chromosomes.
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies documenting ancestry changes.

claim: Populations enter a 'slow' period of purging after the fast period, where selection on individual hybridization-derived haplotypes only subtly shifts genome-wide ancestry proportions.
source: Populations then enter a 'slow' period of purging, where selection on individual hybridization-derived haplotypes only subtly shifts genome-wide ancestry proportions.
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions about long-term ancestry dynamics.

claim: The shape and rate of ancestry change can vary from species to species, primarily as a function of the total recombination rate.
source: The shape and rate of this change in ancestry can vary from species to species (Veller, 2019), primarily as a function of the total recombination rate (see Principle 3).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work on recombination effects.

claim: Regions of the genome that are dense in coding or conserved elements tend to be particularly resistant to movement between species.
source: Although the sources of selection on hybrids undoubtedly differ between species (Juric et al., 2016; Schumer et al., 2018; Brandvain et al., 2014), studies across diverse taxa have largely found that regions of the genome that are dense in coding or conserved elements tend to be particularly resistant to movement between species (Sankararaman et al., 2014; Teeter et al., 2008; Turissini and Matute, 2017; Martin et al., 2013; Calfee, 2021; Brandvain et al., 2014; Masly and Presgraves, 2007; Maxwell et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies across diverse taxa.

claim: In the case of conserved regulatory elements in humans, the pattern of reduced introgression is stronger at enhancers that harbor derived mutations as opposed to ancestral variants.
source: In the case of conserved regulatory elements in humans, this pattern is stronger at enhancers that harbor derived mutations as opposed to ancestral variants (Telis et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to specific study in humans.

claim: Selection against minor parent ancestry generates barriers to introgression that are, in many cases, common, functionally broad, and polygenic.
source: The consistency of the observation that introgression is depleted in functionally important regions implies that selection against minor parent ancestry generates barriers to introgression that are, in many cases, common, functionally broad, and polygenic (Calfee et al., 2020).
evidence: Inferred from consistent observations across species, with citation support.

claim: Introgression is reduced on sex chromosomes.
source: These genome-scale observations echo classic work reporting depleted introgression on sex chromosomes (Martin et al., 2013; Payseur, 2004; Presgraves, 2008) and asymmetry in the effects of hybridization between the sexes (e.g., Orr, 1997; Schilthuizen et al., 2011; Turelli, 1998; Haldane's rule), well-accepted rules in the speciation literature (Masly and Presgraves, 2007) that have been thoroughly reviewed elsewhere (Presgraves, 2008; Payseur and Rieseberg, 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to classic work on sex chromosome introgression.

claim: DMIs are overrepresented on sex chromosomes due to factors such as faster X evolution, meiotic drive, and the importance of X chromosome genes in male fertility.
source: One well-established example is the observation that introgression is reduced on the sex chromosomes, presumably because DMIs are overrepresented on the sex chromosomes, due to factors such as faster X evolution, meiotic drive, and the importance of X chromosome genes in male fertility (Trier et al., 2014; Presgraves, 2008; Maheshwari and Barbash, 2011; Qvarnström and Bailey, 2009; Storchová et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations explaining mechanisms of sex chromosome effects.

claim: Theory predicts that minor-parent ancestry will be more fully removed from regions of the genome with low recombination rates.
source: Even after genome-wide admixture proportions have stabilized, theory predicts that minor-parent ancestry will be more fully removed from regions of the genome with low recombination rates (Wu, 2001; Nachman and Payseur, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on recombination effects.

claim: Data from diverse taxa, including swordtail fishes, humans, monkeyflowers, maize, and Heliconius butterflies, support the prediction that minor-parent ancestry is more fully removed from low recombination rate regions.
source: Data from diverse taxa, including swordtail fishes, humans, monkeyflowers, maize, and Heliconius butterflies (Schumer et al., 2018; Calfee, 2021; Edelman et al., 2019; Brandvain et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2019), support this theoretical prediction (but see Corbett-Detig and Nielsen, 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to empirical studies across taxa.

claim: In humans, recombination rates tend to be locally reduced near genes.
source: For example, in humans, recombination rates tend to be locally reduced near genes (Myers et al., 2005; Coop et al., 2008), resulting in a tendency to purge introgressed DNA near genes driven by both Principles 2 and 3, while in swordtail fishes and birds, recombination rates are elevated near genes (Baker et al., 2017; Singhal et al., 2015), pitting these rules against one another.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of recombination landscapes in humans.

claim: In swordtail fishes and birds, recombination rates are elevated near genes.
source: For example, in humans, recombination rates tend to be locally reduced near genes (Myers et al., 2005; Coop et al., 2008), resulting in a tendency to purge introgressed DNA near genes driven by both Principles 2 and 3, while in swordtail fishes and birds, recombination rates are elevated near genes (Baker et al., 2017; Singhal et al., 2015), pitting these rules against one another.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of recombination landscapes in swordtails and birds.

claim: The recombination landscape evolves rapidly in some taxa.
source: In fact, the rapid evolution of the recombination landscape in some taxa (Auton et al., 2012; Baker et al., 2015) may be another factor contributing to variation in the landscape of introgression across species groups.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies documenting recombination landscape evolution.

claim: Dobzhansky–Muller hybrid incompatibilities (DMIs) occur when mutations that have arisen in each parental species' genome interact negatively in hybrids.
source: Dobzhansky–Muller hybrid incompatibilities (DMIs) occur when mutations that have arisen in each parental species' genome interact negatively in hybrids (Dobzhansky, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to foundational work on DMIs.

claim: DMIs are the best documented and best understood mechanism of selection on hybrids.
source: DMIs are the best documented and best understood mechanism of selection on hybrids.
evidence: Based on assessment of the state of the field.

claim: DMIs can take the form of reciprocal losses following gene duplication or modifications in co-evolving regulatory elements, among other mechanisms.
source: In addition to incompatible substitutions that arise in directly interacting proteins, DMIs can take the form of reciprocal losses following gene duplication or modifications in co-evolving regulatory elements, among other mechanisms (Mack and Nachman, 2017; Dion-Côté and Barbash, 2017; Nguyen et al., 2017; Brucker and Bordenstein, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies documenting various DMI mechanisms.

claim: The loci involved in DMIs identified to date are functionally diverse.
source: The loci involved in DMIs identified to date are functionally diverse (Presgraves, 2010a; Maheshwari and Barbash, 2011; Atanasov et al., 2018; Dujon and Louis, 2017), but existing theory and data have hinted at broader evolutionary forces that drive the emergence of hybrid incompatibilities.
evidence: Supported by citations to reviews and studies of DMI loci.

claim: DMIs are largely expected to locally restrict gene flow by preventing introgression at the incompatible loci and regions linked to them.
source: DMIs are largely expected to locally restrict gene flow by preventing introgression at the incompatible loci and regions linked to them (Teeter et al., 2008; Zuellig and Sweigart, 2018; Macholán et al., 2008; Macholán et al., 2008; Carling and Brumfield, 2009), but can also favor the adaptive introgression of pairs of compatible alleles (Bank et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work on DMI effects.

claim: DMIs can favor the adaptive introgression of pairs of compatible alleles.
source: DMIs are largely expected to locally restrict gene flow by preventing introgression at the incompatible loci and regions linked to them (Teeter et al., 2008; Zuellig and Sweigart, 2018; Macholán et al., 2008; Macholán et al., 2008; Carling and Brumfield, 2009), but can also favor the adaptive introgression of pairs of compatible alleles (Bank et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Certain genes appear to be repeatedly involved in hybrid incompatibilities.
source: Beyond sex chromosomes, certain genes appear to be repeatedly involved in hybrid incompatibilities (Figure 1; Trier et al., 2014; Atanasov et al., 2018; Barr and Fishman, 2010; Chase, 2007; Schartl, 2008; Arévalo, 2020; Smagulova et al., 2016; Davies et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1 showing repeated involvement of xmrk gene.

claim: The gene xmrk independently causes melanoma in hybrids between different swordtail fish species.
source: The gene xmrk independently causes melanoma in hybrids between different swordtail fish species.
evidence: Stated in Figure 1 caption and illustrated in the figure.

claim: In crosses between Xiphophorus birchmanni and Xiphophorus malinche, xmrk interacts with the gene cd97 to generate melanoma in a subset of hybrids.
source: In crosses between Xiphophorus birchmanni and Xiphophorus malinche, xmrk interacts with the gene cd97 to generate melanoma in a subset of hybrids (Powell et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated in Figure 1 caption with citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In crosses between Xiphophorus maculatus and Xiphophorus hellerii, xmrk interacts with a different region, rab3d, to cause melanoma.
source: In crosses between distantly related species Xiphophorus maculatus and Xiphophorus hellerii, xmrk interacts with a different region, rab3d, to cause melanoma (Schartl et al., 2010; Kazianis et al., 1998; Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated in Figure 1 caption with citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses suggest that the incompatibilities with xmrk have arisen independently.
source: Phylogenetic analyses suggest that these incompatibilities with xmrk have arisen independently (Powell et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated in Figure 1 caption with citation.

claim: Selection on introgressed ancestry might reflect the unconditional deleterious effect of a mutation, rather than its poor interaction with other sites in the genome.
source: In other words, selection on introgressed ancestry might reflect the unconditional deleterious effect of a mutation, rather than its poor interaction with other sites in the genome (as seen in DMIs).
evidence: Contrasts hybridization load with DMI model.

claim: Mildly deleterious alleles will preferentially reach fixation in populations with weaker purifying selection, such as those with smaller effective population sizes.
source: Such mildly deleterious alleles will preferentially reach fixation in populations with weaker purifying selection, such as those with smaller effective population sizes.
evidence: Based on established population genetics theory.

claim: With sufficient time, a large number of weakly deleterious mutations can accumulate within a species, which would generate a strong selective force after hybridization with a species that harbors fewer such mutations.
source: With sufficient time, a large number of weakly deleterious mutations can accumulate within a species, which would generate a strong selective force after hybridization with a species that harbors fewer such mutations.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about mutation accumulation.

claim: Hybridization can introduce deleterious mutations at much higher frequencies in the recipient population than expected from mutation-selection balance in the species with higher historical effective population size.
source: In such cases, hybridization can introduce deleterious mutations at much higher frequencies in the recipient population than expected from mutation-selection balance in the species with higher historical effective population size.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about hybridization load effects.

claim: Although each mutation is weakly selected against individually, in aggregate these mutations strongly reduce hybrid fitness relative to populations with fewer deleterious mutations, because they are linked to the same haplotypes after hybridization.
source: Although each mutation is weakly selected against individually, in aggregate these mutations strongly reduce hybrid fitness relative to populations with fewer deleterious mutations, because they are linked to the same haplotypes after hybridization.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about linked selection effects.

claim: After genome-wide admixture proportions have equilibrated, selection against specific deleterious sites may still drive long-term ancestry purging.
source: In the case of a pulse model of admixture, after genome-wide admixture proportions have equilibrated, selection against specific deleterious sites may still drive long-term ancestry purging (see Effects of hybrid demography).
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions about long-term selection.

claim: Empirical studies support the prediction that ancestry from the species with less effective purifying selection can be depleted over many generations of selection, particularly in coding and conserved non-coding regions of the genome.
source: Empirical studies support this prediction, showing that ancestry from the species with less effective purifying selection can be depleted over many generations of selection, particularly in coding and conserved non-coding regions of the genome (Juric et al., 2016; Harris and Nielsen, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The additive hybridization load model predicts selection for directional introgression from the species that harbors fewer deleterious mutations.
source: In contrast to other models, which predict widespread selection against minor parent ancestry, the additive hybridization load model predicts selection for directional introgression from the species that harbors fewer deleterious mutations.
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions of the hybridization load model.

claim: If deleterious mutations are recessive, theory and some empirical data predict that selection will favor an excess of foreign ancestry, especially in the species with lower historical population sizes.
source: Alternatively, if deleterious mutations are recessive, theory and some empirical data predict that selection will favor an excess of foreign ancestry (Box 2; Harris and Nielsen, 2016; Kim, 2017), especially in the species with lower historical population sizes.
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Selection against hybridization load could produce patterns that are distinguishable from other models of selection on hybrids because these weakly deleterious mutations are expected to be broadly distributed throughout the genome and fall within a particular range of selection coefficients.
source: In principle, selection against hybridization load could produce patterns that are distinguishable from other models of selection on hybrids because these weakly deleterious mutations are expected to be broadly distributed throughout the genome and fall within a particular range of selection coefficients (Box 1; Juric et al., 2016; Harris and Nielsen, 2016).
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions with citation support.

claim: Ecological selection is a potentially important but poorly understood source of selection on hybrids.
source: Ecological selection is a potentially important but poorly understood source of selection on hybrids.
evidence: Assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Hybrids may express ecological traits that are intermediate to those of their parent populations.
source: Hybrids may express ecological traits that are intermediate to those of their parent populations (e.g., Hermansen et al., 2011; Hayden et al., 2011) or express 'phenotypically mismatched' traits (Thompson, 2019a and Box 2).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical examples.

claim: Hybrids may express 'phenotypically mismatched' traits.
source: Hybrids may express ecological traits that are intermediate to those of their parent populations (e.g., Hermansen et al., 2011; Hayden et al., 2011) or express 'phenotypically mismatched' traits (Thompson, 2019a and Box 2).
evidence: Supported by citation.

claim: Ecological selection will disfavor hybrids when they express intermediate or phenotypically mismatched traits.
source: In such cases, ecological selection will disfavor hybrids (Delmore and Irwin, 2014; Linn et al., 2003; Gow et al., 2007; Melo et al., 2014; Soria-Carrasco et al., 2014; Nosil et al., 2005; Scordato et al., 2020), unless hybrids exist in an intermediate ecological niche or an environment favoring these mismatched phenotypes (Schluter, 2000; Stelkens et al., 2009; Rieseberg et al., 1999; Selz and Seehausen, 2019; Hessenauer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Hybrids may not be disfavored by ecological selection if they exist in an intermediate ecological niche or an environment favoring mismatched phenotypes.
source: In such cases, ecological selection will disfavor hybrids (Delmore and Irwin, 2014; Linn et al., 2003; Gow et al., 2007; Melo et al., 2014; Soria-Carrasco et al., 2014; Nosil et al., 2005; Scordato et al., 2020), unless hybrids exist in an intermediate ecological niche or an environment favoring these mismatched phenotypes (Schluter, 2000; Stelkens et al., 2009; Rieseberg et al., 1999; Selz and Seehausen, 2019; Hessenauer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing context-dependent hybrid fitness.

claim: Ecological selection is predicted to result in biased ancestry around functionally relevant genomic regions, though the expected direction of bias depends on the environment.
source: Like the DMI and hybridization load models, ecological selection is predicted to result in biased ancestry around functionally relevant genomic regions, though the expected direction of bias depends on the environment (Box 1).
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions about ecological selection effects.

claim: In Fisher's geometric model of polygenic adaptation, individual fitness in the parental species can be described as a function of distance from a phenotypic optimum in quantitative trait space.
source: In a Fisherian model of polygenic adaptation, individual fitness in the parental species can be described as a function of distance from a phenotypic optimum in quantitative trait space, and isolated populations maintain their respective optima through the independent fixation of sets of trait-increasing and trait-decreasing alleles (Tenaillon, 2014).
evidence: Describes Fisher's geometric model with citation.

claim: Given enough time, the sets of loci underlying a trait and the sign of their phenotypic effects are likely to differ across populations, even between populations with identical phenotypic optima.
source: Crucially, given enough time, the sets of loci underlying the trait and the sign of their phenotypic effects are likely to differ across populations, even between populations with identical phenotypic optima (Slatkin and Lande, 1994; Barton, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: In hybrids, recombination decouples sets of parental alleles, which can result in hybrid phenotypes that fall outside of the phenotypic optima of either parental species.
source: In hybrids, recombination decouples these sets of parental alleles. This can result in hybrid phenotypes that fall outside of the phenotypic optima of either parental species, reducing fitness through a phenomenon known as segregation load (Barton, 1989; Slatkin and Lande, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on segregation load.

claim: When parental alleles are mixed into different genetic backgrounds, hybrids can show greater variance in a trait than observed in either of the parental species.
source: More precisely, when parental alleles are mixed into different genetic backgrounds, hybrids can show greater variance in a trait than observed in either of the parental species (Figure 2).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: If a trait is under stabilizing selection in hybrids, increased variance in that trait could drive purging of minor parent ancestry over time.
source: If the trait is also under stabilizing selection in hybrids, this increased variance could drive purging of minor parent ancestry over time.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about stabilizing selection effects.

claim: Predictions about increased trait variance in hybrids should hold when parental species are adapting to similar or distinct phenotypic optima.
source: Notably, these predictions should hold when parental species are adapting to similar (Melo, 2019) or distinct (Walter et al., 2020) phenotypic optima (Figure 2), and when genotypic effects are non-additive (Schneemann, 2019; Fierst and Hansen, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Predictions about increased trait variance in hybrids should hold when genotypic effects are non-additive.
source: Notably, these predictions should hold when parental species are adapting to similar (Melo, 2019) or distinct (Walter et al., 2020) phenotypic optima (Figure 2), and when genotypic effects are non-additive (Schneemann, 2019; Fierst and Hansen, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Haplotypes introduced by hybridization can confer an adaptive advantage.
source: There is no doubt that haplotypes introduced by hybridization can confer an adaptive advantage (Hedrick, 2013; Racimo et al., 2015; Song et al., 2011; Heliconius Genome Consortium, 2012; Norris et al., 2015; Feurtey et al., 2019; Corcoran et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Adaptive introgression increases minor parent ancestry locally around the adaptive allele.
source: Intuitively, adaptive introgression increases minor parent ancestry locally around the adaptive allele.
evidence: Based on intuitive reasoning about selection effects.

claim: The footprint of peaks in minor parent ancestry around adaptive alleles is expected to be positively correlated with the selection coefficient in the absence of negative selection on linked sites.
source: The footprint of these peaks in minor parent ancestry is expected to be positively correlated with the selection coefficient in the absence of negative selection on linked sites (see below).
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions about selective sweep signatures.

claim: Adaptive haplotypes can be shorter in certain demographic scenarios, since they persist longer in hybrid populations, leaving more time for them to be broken up by recombination.
source: However, adaptive haplotypes can actually be shorter in certain demographic scenarios, since they persist longer in hybrid populations, leaving more time for them to be broken up by recombination (Sedghifar et al., 2016; Shchur et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: As an adaptive haplotype sweeps to fixation, it drives minor parent ancestry to intermediate frequency in large flanking regions, creating a 'volcano-shaped' signature of genetic diversity approaching the site under positive selection.
source: As an adaptive haplotype sweeps to fixation, it drives minor parent ancestry to intermediate frequency in large flanking regions, creating a 'volcano-shaped' signature of genetic diversity approaching the site under positive selection (Setter et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: The volcano-shaped signature is generated because recombination events that shorten the haplotype but still contain the adaptive allele are retained during the sweep, resulting in a concentration of ancestry heterozygosity at the edges of a fixed adaptive haplotype.
source: This shape is generated because recombination events that shorten the haplotype but still contain the adaptive allele are retained during the sweep, resulting in a concentration of ancestry heterozygosity at the edges of a fixed adaptive haplotype (Setter et al., 2019; Moest et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations explaining the mechanism.

claim: Adaptive introgression is often occurring against a background of genome-wide purging.
source: Given broad selection against minor parent ancestry, adaptive introgression is often occurring against a background of genome-wide purging (Calfee, 2021; Edelman et al., 2019; Turner and Harr, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Adaptively introgressed haplotypes are sometimes easy to identify empirically since they form peaks of high minor parent ancestry against a background of low minor parent ancestry.
source: In some cases, this has made adaptively introgressed haplotypes easy to identify empirically since they form peaks of high minor parent ancestry against a background of low minor parent ancestry (Sankararaman et al., 2014; Vernot and Akey, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Several factors will impact the probability that a globally adaptive allele will introgress between species, including the locations of potentially adaptive alleles relative to deleterious neighbors, the relative selection coefficients on adaptive and deleterious sites, and other features of genome organization.
source: This also means that several factors will impact the probability that a globally adaptive allele will introgress between species. These include the locations of potentially adaptive alleles relative to deleterious neighbors, the relative selection coefficients on adaptive and deleterious sites, and other features of genome organization (Veller, 2019).
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning with citation support.

claim: An adaptive haplotype in a region of the genome with a very low recombination rate would have a lower probability of introgressing than a haplotype with the same advantage in a higher recombination rate region.
source: For example, an adaptive haplotype in a region of the genome with a very low recombination rate would have a lower probability of introgressing than a haplotype with the same advantage in a higher recombination rate region (Principle 3).
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions from first principles.

claim: In the admixture event between humans and Neanderthals, both hybridization load and adaptive introgression have shaped Neanderthal ancestry in modern human genomes.
source: Although research to date has largely focused on each mechanism in isolation, most hybridization events likely involve the interplay between several modes of selection. As discussed above, in the admixture event between humans and Neanderthals, both hybridization load and adaptive introgression have shaped Neanderthal ancestry in modern human genomes (Sankararaman et al., 2014; Juric et al., 2016; Harris and Nielsen, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of human-Neanderthal admixture.

claim: The combination of positive and negative selection on hybridization-derived haplotypes can generate interference, especially in the early generations following hybridization when long haplotypes of each ancestry type are common.
source: This combination of positive and negative selection on hybridization-derived haplotypes can generate interference, especially in the early generations following hybridization when long haplotypes of each ancestry type are common (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: It may be possible to disentangle different signals of selection on hybrids using local ancestry variation or changes in ancestry over time.
source: Simulations hint that it may be possible to disentangle different signals of selection on hybrids using local ancestry variation (Figure 3) or changes in ancestry over time (Figure 4; Uecker et al., 2015), presenting exciting opportunities for future work.
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in Figures 3 and 4, with citation.

claim: Replicated hybridization events between the same species lead to predictable outcomes at the genomic level.
source: Moving beyond these broad-scale features, there are good reasons to expect that replicated hybridization events between the same species will lead to predictable outcomes at the genomic level. In repeated hybridization events between the same species, the same genetic interactions and selective forces are predicted to drive concordant changes in ancestry along the genome. Indeed, this has been observed in experimental hybrid populations, natural hybrid populations (Schumer et al., 2018; Chaturvedi et al., 2020; Matute et al., 2020; Calfee et al., 2020; Kovach et al., 2016; Bay et al., 2019; Hufford et al., 2013; Riquet et al., 2019; Smukowski Heil et al., 2019), and in replicated cline studies (Westram et al., 2021; but see Nolte et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to empirical studies showing repeatability.

claim: Studies in Arabidopsis and Xiphophorus have repeatedly uncovered some of the same genes underlying hybrid incompatibilities.
source: Studies in Arabidopsis and Xiphophorus have repeatedly uncovered some of the same genes underlying hybrid incompatibilities (Figure 1; Chae et al., 2014; Alcázar et al., 2014; Powell et al., 2020; Schartl et al., 2010), and certain genetic interactions, such as cytonuclear incompatibilities, are common across the tree of life (Chase, 2007; Hill, 2017; Bar-Yaacov et al., 2015; Beresford et al., 2017; Bolnick et al., 2008; Burton and Barreto, 2012; He et al., 2020; McDaniel et al., 2007; Giordano et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Cytonuclear incompatibilities are common across the tree of life.
source: Studies in Arabidopsis and Xiphophorus have repeatedly uncovered some of the same genes underlying hybrid incompatibilities (Figure 1; Chae et al., 2014; Alcázar et al., 2014; Powell et al., 2020; Schartl et al., 2010), and certain genetic interactions, such as cytonuclear incompatibilities, are common across the tree of life (Chase, 2007; Hill, 2017; Bar-Yaacov et al., 2015; Beresford et al., 2017; Bolnick et al., 2008; Burton and Barreto, 2012; He et al., 2020; McDaniel et al., 2007; Giordano et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations across diverse taxa.

claim: Comparisons of dynamics of adaptive introgression across species have identified possible hotspots in terms of gene families that appear to confer advantages when introgressed.
source: Similarly, comparisons of dynamics of adaptive introgression across species have identified possible hotspots in terms of gene families that appear to confer advantages when introgressed.
evidence: Based on synthesis of comparative studies.

claim: The best documented examples of gene families that confer advantages when introgressed include immune-related genes, pigmentation genes, and genes that underlie resistance.
source: The best documented examples include immune-related genes (Sankararaman et al., 2014; Enard and Petrov, 2018; Fijarczyk et al., 2018), pigmentation genes (Moest et al., 2020; Vickrey et al., 2018; Giska et al., 2019; Jones et al., 2018; Rotival and Quintana-Murci, 2020; Stryjewski and Sorenson, 2017; Wallbank et al., 2016), and genes that underlie resistance (Song et al., 2011; Lindtke et al., 2013; Norris et al., 2015; Bechsgaard et al., 2017; Whitney et al., 2006; Ford et al., 2015), but many other functional categories of genes or selfish elements could have similar behavior (Staubach et al., 2012; Meiklejohn et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Selection against hybridization load could lead to partially predictable outcomes across replicated hybridization events.
source: Although this has not been directly studied, selection against hybridization load could lead to partially predictable outcomes across replicated hybridization events.
evidence: Based on theoretical speculation about hybridization load effects.

claim: Regions of the genome with lower local Ne should accumulate more weakly deleterious mutations within populations and thus be more likely to be purged after hybridization.
source: Regions of the genome with lower local Ne (i.e., due to variation in the effects of background selection; McVicker et al., 2009; Elyashiv et al., 2016) should accumulate more weakly deleterious mutations within populations and thus be more likely to be purged after hybridization.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning with citation support.

claim: Gene-dense regions provide a larger target for functionally relevant mutations to occur and may therefore experience stronger selection in the early generations after hybridization when ancestry tracts are long.
source: Additionally, gene-dense regions provide a larger target for functionally relevant mutations to occur and may therefore experience stronger selection in the early generations after hybridization when ancestry tracts are long.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about mutation target size.

claim: There are differences in the extent to which introgressed haplotypes were retained in coding regions in the genomes of swordtail fishes and humans, likely due to differences in the underlying recombination maps.
source: We recently found differences in the extent to which introgressed haplotypes were retained in coding regions in the genomes of swordtail fishes and humans, likely due to differences in the underlying recombination maps (Schumer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study.

claim: Both swordtail fishes and humans share a strong positive correlation between introgression and the local recombination rate.
source: Both species share a strong positive correlation between introgression and the local recombination rate.
evidence: Based on empirical observations in both species.

claim: Recombination is concentrated in promoters and other functional regions in swordtail fishes.
source: However, recombination is concentrated in promoters and other functional regions in swordtail fishes (Baker et al., 2017), and tends to occur away from such regions in humans (Myers et al., 2005; Coop et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to study of swordtail recombination.

claim: Swordtail fishes retain more minor parent ancestry than humans in and around genes, presumably due to differing outcomes of the action of Principles 2 and 3 in the two species groups.
source: This results in distinct patterns of local ancestry, with swordtail fishes retaining more minor parent ancestry than humans in and around genes (presumably due to differing outcomes of the action of Principles 2 and 3 in the two species groups).
evidence: Based on comparative analysis with inference about mechanisms.

claim: The speed of initial purging of minor parent ancestry is sensitive to the aggregate recombination rate, which differs widely between species.
source: Similarly, as discussed in Principle 1, the speed of initial purging of minor parent ancestry is sensitive to the aggregate recombination rate, which differs widely between species (Veller, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: The aggregate recombination rate is strongly influenced by the total number of chromosomes and whether recombination occurs in both sexes.
source: This is because the aggregate recombination rate is strongly influenced by the total number of chromosomes and whether recombination occurs in both sexes – properties that vary widely across the tree of life (Veller, 2019; Stapley et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations explaining factors affecting recombination rate.

claim: Factors affecting aggregate recombination rate may be important in explaining the variation in admixture proportions observed in the genomes of different species that are known to commonly hybridize.
source: Notably, these factors together may be important in explaining the variation in admixture proportions observed in the genomes of different species that are known to commonly hybridize, from cases where retention of minor parent ancestry after hybridization is rare, such as Drosophila (Coyne and Orr, 2004), to those where extensive introgression is common, such as swordtail fishes (Cui, 2013).
evidence: Based on inference from theoretical predictions with citation support.

claim: Pulses of hybridization may coincide with strong bottlenecks since they are often driven by ecological disturbance.
source: However, there are multiple reasons to predict that pulses of hybridization may coincide with strong bottlenecks since they are often driven by ecological disturbance (Fisher et al., 2006; Chunco, 2014) and because selection on hybrids can be so strong that it essentially drives population collapse (Shorter et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on hybridization and demography.

claim: Selection on hybrids can be so strong that it essentially drives population collapse.
source: However, there are multiple reasons to predict that pulses of hybridization may coincide with strong bottlenecks since they are often driven by ecological disturbance (Fisher et al., 2006; Chunco, 2014) and because selection on hybrids can be so strong that it essentially drives population collapse (Shorter et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study.

claim: Over long time periods, populations with a small effective size will be less efficient at purging weakly deleterious variants that occur in short ancestry tracts.
source: Over long time periods, however, populations with a small effective size will be less efficient at purging weakly deleterious variants that occur in short ancestry tracts.
evidence: Based on population genetics theory about drift and selection.

claim: The number of parental individuals from each species that contributed to a hybridization event will shape the raw material on which selection can act.
source: Another important consideration is the number of parental individuals from each species that contributed to a hybridization event, which will shape the raw material on which selection can act.
evidence: Based on reasoning about founder effects.

claim: A tail pigmentation spot that causes hybrid melanoma in swordtail fishes is polymorphic in one of the parental species at approximately 30% frequency.
source: We recently mapped the genetic basis of a hybrid melanoma that develops from a tail pigmentation spot in swordtail fishes. Notably, this tail pigmentation spot is polymorphic in one of the parental species (~30% frequency; Powell et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study.

claim: Due to differences in the founding parental populations, some swordtail hybrid populations have both a high frequency of the tail spot and of melanoma, whereas others have a low frequency of both.
source: Presumably due to differences in the founding parental populations, some hybrid populations have both a high frequency of the tail spot and of melanoma, whereas others have a low frequency of both (Powell et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation with inference about mechanism.

claim: Studies in Drosophila, Mimulus, Mus, and Caenorhabditis elegans have identified polymorphic hybrid incompatibilities.
source: Studies in other systems such as Drosophila, Mimulus, Mus, and Caenorhabditis elegans have identified polymorphic hybrid incompatibilities, suggesting that these founder dynamics could have important impacts on hybrid populations (Zuellig and Sweigart, 2018; Corbett-Detig et al., 2013; Cutter, 2012; Larson et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2012; Good, 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Distinct demographic histories in hybrid populations or variation in genetic contributions from the parental species could drive differences in local ancestry between populations.
source: These factors will also impact the repeatability and predictability of genome evolution after hybridization. Distinct demographic histories in hybrid populations or variation in genetic contributions from the parental species could drive differences in local ancestry between populations by shaping features such as the distribution of ancestry tract lengths and the efficacy of selection.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about demographic effects.

claim: Whether demographic differences will substantially limit repeatability in local ancestry in replicate hybrid populations will depend in part on the strength of selection relative to demographic forces such as genetic drift.
source: Whether demographic differences will substantially limit repeatability in local ancestry in replicate hybrid populations will depend in part on the strength of selection relative to demographic forces such as genetic drift.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about selection-drift balance.

claim: If the mutations that cause DMIs are enriched in the same genes or genomic regions, the rate of accumulation of incompatibilities should slow.
source: However, if the mutations that cause DMIs are enriched in the same genes or genomic regions, the rate of this accumulation should slow (Kalirad and Azevedo, 2017; Maya-Lastra and Eaton, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: The likelihood of a gene's involvement in DMIs is directly related to the density of the gene network.
source: Similar predictions emerge from theoretical studies of gene regulatory network evolution, where the likelihood of a gene's involvement in DMIs is directly related to the density of the gene network (Yang and Scarpino, 2020; Satokangas, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on network evolution.

claim: Systematic differences in gene network connectivity between species could drive differences in the distribution of DMIs across the tree of life.
source: Systematic differences in gene network connectivity between species could drive differences in the distribution of DMIs across the tree of life (Cutter and Bundus, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation with inference about implications.

claim: Selection on DMIs is generally thought to be stronger and less polygenic than hybridization load models.
source: Selection on DMIs is generally thought to be stronger and less polygenic than hybridization load models (Box 1; but empirical evidence is lacking, see Fierst and Hansen, 2010 for an exploration of polygenic epistatic selection).
evidence: Based on theoretical understanding with citation noting lack of empirical evidence.

claim: Higher levels of polygenicity will increase the proportion of neutral basepairs that are linked to sites that are deleterious in hybrids.
source: Higher levels of polygenicity will increase the proportion of neutral basepairs that are linked to sites that are deleterious in hybrids (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Under a DMI model ancestral and transitional genotypes can be favored by selection, which will actually act to increase minor parent ancestry in some regions of the genome.
source: Moreover, under a DMI model ancestral and transitional genotypes can be favored by selection, which will actually act to increase minor parent ancestry in some regions of the genome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on theoretical predictions illustrated in supplementary figure.

claim: Polygenic models of selection against minor parent ancestry lead to greater purging of minor parent ancestry over time compared to classic DMI models.
source: Together these factors will lead to greater purging of minor parent ancestry over time under polygenic models of selection against minor parent ancestry, as opposed to classic DMI models (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Chen et al. found that genome-wide selection broadly favored ancestry derived from migrants in small populations, consistent with the idea that in small populations foreign ancestry can be favored to lighten the genetic load.
source: For example, Chen et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2016 and Fitzpatrick, 2019 studied weakly differentiated populations and found that genome-wide selection broadly favored ancestry derived from migrants in small populations, consistent with the idea that in small populations foreign ancestry can be favored to lighten the genetic load.
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: There is little evidence that hybridization load shapes genome-wide ancestry in hybrid swordtail populations formed between species with substantial differences in historical effective population size.
source: In contrast, we recently found little evidence that hybridization load shapes genome-wide ancestry in hybrid swordtail populations formed between species with substantial differences in historical effective population size (Schumer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study.

claim: Hybrids may have different recombination landscapes than their parental species due to features such as structural differences between species that suppress recombination, dysfunction in the recombination process, recombination modifiers, or different hotspot usage in hybrids compared to the parental species.
source: It is also possible that hybrids will have different recombination landscapes than their parental species due to features such as structural differences between species that suppress recombination (Kirkpatrick, 2010), dysfunction in the recombination process (Davies et al., 2016), recombination modifiers (Brand et al., 2018), or different hotspot usage in hybrids compared to the parental species (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies of various mechanisms.

claim: Theory predicts that species with fewer chromosomes will undergo faster and stronger purging of minor parent ancestry in their genomes, due to a low aggregate recombination rate.
source: For one, theory predicts that species with fewer chromosomes will undergo faster and stronger purging of minor parent ancestry in their genomes, due to a low aggregate recombination rate (Veller, 2019, e.g., in species such as Arabidopsis, Drosophila, mosquitoes).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work with examples.

claim: The extent of selfing or asexual reproduction impacts the genetic diversity of the parent populations, their genetic load, and the frequency with which recombination reshuffles parental haplotypes, and therefore can shape the extent and direction of introgression.
source: For example, the extent of selfing or asexual reproduction impacts the genetic diversity of the parent populations, their genetic load, and the frequency with which recombination reshuffles parental haplotypes, and therefore can shape the extent and direction of introgression (Pickup et al., 2019; Hamlin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mating system effects.

claim: Some data suggest that systems with facultative asexual reproduction can retain larger minor parent contributions.
source: Similarly, some data suggest that systems with facultative asexual reproduction can retain larger minor parent contributions (Langdon et al., 2019; Marcet-Houben and Gabaldón, 2015; Gallone et al., 2019), and tolerance of genome duplication and aneuploidy will interplay with retention or loss of parental genomic material (Steensels et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Inversions play an important role in locally restricting or promoting gene flow.
source: Decades of work have established an important role for inversions in locally restricting (or promoting; Edelman et al., 2019; Jay et al., 2018; Todesco et al., 2020) gene flow (Noor et al., 2001; Wellenreuther and Bernatchez, 2018; Kirkpatrick and Barton, 2006; Faria et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on inversion effects.

claim: There is weaker selection against Neanderthal ancestry in enhancers that are tissue specific in modern humans.
source: Notably, recent work has demonstrated that there is weaker selection against Neanderthal ancestry in enhancers that are tissue specific in modern humans (Telis et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to empirical study.

claim: tspan8 and pkma are examples of genes for which swordtail hybrids exhibit low and high misexpression, respectively.
source: tspan8 (left) and pkma (right) are examples of genes for which swordtail hybrids exhibit low and high misexpression, respectively (MM: X. malinche; BB: X. birchmanni; MB: F1 hybrids; data from Powell et al., 2021).
evidence: Stated in Figure 5 caption with citation and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mismatches in co-evolved regulatory elements can cause misexpression in hybrids.
source: This simplified diagram illustrates how mismatches in co-evolved regulatory elements can cause misexpression.
evidence: Stated in Figure 5 caption and illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: In hybrids, divergent binding sites within the promoter and changes in binding affinity of the transcription factor may result in over- or underexpression of target genes, leading to misexpression.
source: In hybrids, divergent binding sites within the promoter and changes in binding affinity of the TF may result in over- or underexpression of target genes, leading to misexpression (bottom).
evidence: Stated in Figure 5 caption and illustrated in Figure 5B.
